Consider the arc of the curve $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ that lies between $y=0$ and $y=\frac{\pi }{2},$ as shown above. What integral gives the area of the surface generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡y)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\sqrt{1+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡y)}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\sqrt{1+{sin}^{2}⁡y}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the arc of the curve $x=y-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}$ that lies to the right of the $y$-axis between its $y$-intercepts. What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2} & =0 \\ 2y-{y}^{2} & =0 \\ y(2-y) & =0 \\ y & =0,2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=2.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(y-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2})=1-y.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(y-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2})\sqrt{1+{(1-y)}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(y-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2})\sqrt{1+(1-2y+{y}^{2})}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(y-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2})\sqrt{2-2y+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from $y=1$ to $y=e.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=\frac{1}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}3+2y-{y}^{2} & =0 \\ {y}^{2}-2y-3 & =0 \\ (y+1)(y-3) & =0 \\ y & =-1,3\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $y=-1$ to $y=3.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(3+2y-{y}^{2})=2-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$

$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $x$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-4x+3 & =0 \\ (x-1)(x-3) & =0 \\ x & =1,3\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=1$ to $x=3.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-4x+3)=2x-4.\end{aligned}

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Surface Area of Revolution
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1+{x}^{2})=2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}=4{x}^{2}.
$$

Then, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}x\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=1+4{x}^{2}.$ Then, $8x\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.$

We also need to compute new limits:

| **$x$** | $0$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $2$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}x\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{8}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{2}{u}^{1/2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{[\frac{2{u}^{3/2}}{3}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}[(2)^{3/2}-(1)^{3/2}] \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(2\sqrt{2}-1) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(2\sqrt{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the arc of the curve $x=\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}$ that lies between the lines $y=0$ and $y=\sqrt{2}.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{-2y}{2\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}} \\  & =-\frac{y}{\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{4-{y}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}\sqrt{1+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}\sqrt{\frac{4}{4-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}2\,\text{d}y \\  & =4\pi \,y{|}_{0}^{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =4\pi (\sqrt{2}-0) \\  & =4\pi \sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the arc of the curve $y={(4-{x}^{2/3})}^{3/2}$ that lies between the lines $x=0$ and $x=1.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[{(4-{x}^{2/3})}^{3/2}] \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{(4-{x}^{2/3})}^{1/2}(-\frac{2}{3}{x}^{-1/3}) \\  & =-{x}^{-1/3}{(4-{x}^{2/3})}^{1/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}={x}^{-2/3}(4-{x}^{2/3})=4{x}^{-2/3}-1.
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}x\sqrt{1+(4{x}^{-2/3}-1)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}x\sqrt{4{x}^{-2/3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot {x}^{-1/3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2/3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\pi {[\frac{3}{5}{x}^{5/3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{12\pi }{5}(1-0) \\  & =\frac{12\pi }{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the arc of the curve $x=\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}$ that lies between the lines $y=0$ and $y=\sqrt[4]{3}.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}) \\  & ={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}={y}^{4}.
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{3}}\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}\sqrt{1+{y}^{4}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{3}}{y}^{3}\sqrt{1+{y}^{4}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=1+{y}^{4}.$ Then, ${y}^{3}\text{d}y=(\frac{1}{4})\text{d}u.$

We also need to compute new limits:

| **$x$** | $0$ | $\sqrt[4]{3}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $4$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =\frac{2\pi }{3}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{3}}{y}^{3}\sqrt{1+{y}^{4}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}{\int }_{1}^{4}{u}^{1/2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}{[\frac{2{u}^{3/2}}{3}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}[\frac{2(4)^{3/2}}{3}-\frac{2(1)^{3/2}}{3}] \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(\frac{16}{3}-\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(\frac{14}{3}) \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the arc of the curve $y=\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3/2}$ that lies between the lines $x=0$ and $x=3.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3/2})={x}^{1/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}=x.
$$

Then, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}x\sqrt{1+x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=1+x.$ Then, $\text{d}x=\text{d}u.$

We also need to compute new limits:

| **$x$** | $0$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $4$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}x\sqrt{1+x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{4}(u-1)\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{4}({u}^{3/2}-{u}^{1/2})\text{d}u \\  & =2\pi {[\frac{2{u}^{5/2}}{5}-\frac{2{u}^{3/2}}{3}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =2\pi [\frac{2(4)^{5/2}}{5}-\frac{2(4)^{3/2}}{3}-(\frac{2(1)^{5/2}}{5}-\frac{2(1)^{3/2}}{3})] \\  & =2\pi (\frac{64}{5}-\frac{16}{3}-\frac{2}{5}+\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =2\pi (\frac{116}{15}) \\  & =\frac{232\pi }{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Integrals Representing Surface Areas Generated by Functions of Y
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the arc of the curve $x=y^2$ that lies between $y=0$ and $y=2,$ as shown below. What integral gives the area of the surface generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14082799/assets/30c2b0000055802166e5bdf8ec3e305d83e65ac960043f66463702952d91e4d6.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S = \int 2\pi x\,\textrm d s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x = f(y),$ we have 

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d y}\right)^2}\,\textrm d y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{y_1}^{y_2} x \sqrt{1+ \left( \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}y.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=2.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2})=2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}({y}^{2})\sqrt{1+{(2y)}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}\sqrt{1+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the arc of the curve $y=x^3-3x$ that lies in the fourth quadrant between its $x$-intercepts. What integral gives the area of the surface generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14082799/assets/777c36689da6f6cbcf4ce92a7c5ba17c000a7c442a972851d9d1cafaa9fb2ba4.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S = \int 2\pi x\,\textrm d s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y = f(x),$ we have 

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}\right)^2}\,\textrm d x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{x_1}^{x_2} x \sqrt{1+ \left( \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-3x & =0 \\ x({x}^{2}-3) & =0 \\ x & =0,\pm \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x= \sqrt{3}.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}-3x)=3{x}^{2}-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}x\sqrt{1+(3{x}^{2}-3)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}x\sqrt{9{x}^{4}-18{x}^{2}+10}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Consider the segment of the line $y = 2x$ that lies between the lines $x = 0$ and $x = 2.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this segment is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S = \int 2\pi x\,\textrm d s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y = f(x),$ we have 

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}\right)^2}\,\textrm d x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{x_1}^{x_2} x\sqrt{1 + \left( \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \right)^2} \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x)=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\left( \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \right)^2 = 4.
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}x\sqrt{1+4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi \sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{2}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi \sqrt{5}{[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2\pi \sqrt{5}[\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}] \\  & =4\pi \sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$
